cards.claim: Newton-Schulz polynomial degree controls convergence rate gap to ideal SVD method, with larger degree reducing that gap faster
cards.conditions: Nonconvex smooth objectives with bounded stochastic gradient variance; matrix-structured parameters; convergence measured by nuclear-norm stationarity
cards.effect: Polar approximation error decays as exp(-2^d) where d is polynomial degree; the constant factor α(k,d) multiplying convergence rate vanishes doubly exponentially in Newton-Schulz steps k and improves monotonically with degree d
cards.evidence: Theorem 2 and Lemma 3 prove upper bound; numerical ablation on CIFAR-10 with CifarNet (0.35M params, 50 epochs, batch 256) and additional scales (MLP on MNIST, ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100, WideResNet on Tiny-ImageNet, NanoGPT and 1.3B GPT-2 on FineWeb)
cards.quote: Theorem 2 shows that α_k is bounded by α(k,d) = C_d · 2^(-2^k). Hence, α_k vanishes doubly exponentially in k (and improves with larger d)... We further analyze this constant factor and prove that it converges to 1 doubly exponentially in [k] and improves with the degree of the polynomial used in Newton–Schulz for approximating the orthogonalization direction.

cards.claim: Newton-Schulz polynomial degree induces time-accuracy trade-off: increasing degree improves convergence speed per epoch but increases per-step computation
cards.conditions: Multiple datasets and model scales (MNIST 0.5M params, CIFAR-100 11.2M, Tiny-ImageNet 36.6M, FineWeb 124M Transformer and 1.3B GPT-2); polynomial evaluation cost grows with degree
cards.effect: Training loss drops faster at fixed epoch count with higher degree, but wall-clock time per step increases due to more polynomial evaluations; net effect depends on compute cost of polynomial evaluation
cards.evidence: Ablation experiment (Appendix H.1) varying polynomial degree d while fixing k=3 Newton-Schulz steps, plotted for train/test loss and wall-clock cumulative time
cards.quote: Ablation on Newton–Schulz polynomial degree. We perform a controlled ablation that varies the degree of the Newton–Schulz polynomial while fixing the number of Newton–Schulz steps to [k=3] for all variants. Increasing the degree improves optimization (the loss drops faster at a fixed epoch) but lengthens each step, yielding a clear accuracy–time trade-off

cards.claim: Few Newton-Schulz steps (even k=1 or 2) suffice to match SVD-based orthogonalization in iteration complexity, making Newton-Schulz attractive despite approximation
cards.conditions: Nonconvex smooth objectives; matrix parameters; k Newton-Schulz steps compared to exact SVD polar decomposition; iteration complexity metric
cards.effect: Iteration count to reach ε-stationarity increases by factor α(k,d) which is ≤ 4 for k=1, ≤ 2.8 for k=2, decaying doubly exponentially toward 1; empirically k=2 achieves near-identical loss curves to SVD variant
cards.evidence: Theorem 1 and 2; numerical experiment on CIFAR-10 (Figure 1 top row) shows Muon with k=2 Newton-Schulz steps matches SVD variant loss curves nearly exactly for both train and test loss over 50 epochs
cards.quote: with only a few Newton–Schulz steps, the convergence rate of Muon quickly tends to the convergence rate of the exact polar step via SVD... Muon with [k=2] already outperforms SGD-M, and nearly coincides with the SVD-based Muon in both train loss and test loss, in line with Theorems 1 and 2

cards.claim: Newton-Schulz orthogonalization removes matrix-rank dependence penalty that vector-based optimizers incur
cards.conditions: Matrix-structured parameters; comparison to SGD with momentum; convergence measured under nuclear-norm stationarity metric; rank k_r of momentum matrix varies
cards.effect: SGD with momentum convergence rate scales as O(√k_r) in rank dependence; Muon with Newton-Schulz removes this √k_r factor, making convergence nearly flat in log-log rank plot. Empirical: SGD-M slope ≈0.5 in log-log, Muon variants ≈0 (flat)
cards.evidence: Theorem 3 (SGD-M) vs Theorem 1 (Muon with Newton-Schulz) showing explicit √r factor in SGD-M but not in Muon; rank-dependence ablation (Appendix H.2) showing log-log scaling with monitored layer's effective rank, averaged over epochs
cards.quote: demonstrate for the first time that Muon with Newton–Schulz sharpens the convergence rate by a factor of the square root of the rank of the momentum matrix... SGD-M shows a positive slope of approximately [0.5] (grows with rank), whereas Muon and its variants are nearly flat. These observations are precisely in line with Theorem 3 and Theorem 4

cards.claim: Newton-Schulz approximation cost per iteration is lower than SVD, enabling superior wall-clock convergence despite matching iteration complexity
cards.conditions: Large matrix parameters (up to 1.3B in GPT-2); per-iteration cost dominated by matrix multiplications for Newton-Schulz vs SVD cost; wall-clock time metric
cards.effect: Muon with Newton-Schulz reaches target test loss in substantially less wall-clock time than SVD variant despite nearly identical iteration counts. On CIFAR-10: k=2 reaches same accuracy ~4-5x faster in cumulative wall-clock time (Figure 1 bottom right)
cards.evidence: Numerical experiments on CIFAR-10 (Figure 1 bottom row), MNIST, CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet, NanoGPT (124M), GPT-2 1.3B showing wall-clock time comparisons. per-iteration cost: SVD is O(n³) for n×n matrix; Newton-Schulz is O(k × n²) for k steps and matrix multiplications
cards.quote: each Newton–Schulz step uses only matrix multiplications (and avoids SVD), the per-iteration cost is much lower, which explains the superior wall-clock performance of the original SVD-free Muon observed in practice... Muon with [k=2 or 3] reaches a given test loss substantially faster in wall-clock time than the SVD variant
